quests.instruction: Which two words would sound broken if you stopped between them?
quests.hint: Only one pair in this sentence joins smoothly. Say it at normal speed and notice where your voice refuses to stop.
quests.explanation: 'Left' ends in /ft/ and 'early' begins with a vowel, so the /t/ flows straight on. A pause there turns a casual remark into something that sounds read from a card. The other boundaries leave a natural gap anyway.
quests.flowRule: Smooth versus separated speech: Fluent speakers keep a phrase in one flow and pause only between thought groups. A gap inside a linked pair sounds choppy even when every word is clear, so train your ear to hear the join rather than the separate words.

quests.hint: Say each vowel-letter word on its own and listen to its first sound. One starts with a consonant sound.
quests.explanation: 'Ate one' looks as if it could link, but 'one' begins with /w/ ('wun'), so /t/ meets /w/, two consonants. The real link in the sentence is 'one each', where /n/ runs into /iː/. Spelling invites a link that the sounds do not make.

quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Where does a final /t/, /d/ or /n/ shift to match the next sound?
quests.hint: Which pair's first word changes its last sound to match the next?
quests.explanation: Before /m/ the /n/ of 'on' often becomes /m/, giving 'om Monday'. 'Meet on' is a normal consonant-to-vowel link through /t/.
quests.flowRule: Place assimilation (informal speech): At the end of a word, /t/, /d/ and /n/ often take on the place of the next sound. Before /p b m/ they shift towards lip sounds (ten people sounds like 'tem people'; bad back like 'bab back'), and before /k g/ towards back-of-the-mouth sounds (in case like 'ing case'). It is common in fast speech and listeners barely notice it.

quests.instruction: Which pair could be misheard as different words because the link hides the gap?

quests.hint: One link could be misheard as a different pair of words. Which one hides a gap?
quests.explanation: 'An aim' (/ən eɪm/) and 'a name' (/ə neɪm/) sound almost the same, because linking carries the /n/ across and removes the gap. Context and stress, not the stream of sound, tell you which was meant.
quests.flowRule: Misleading segmentation: The same stream of sounds can be split into different words (an aim / a name, at all / a tall). Linking removes the clear gaps that spelling shows, so context, grammar and stress decide which words were meant.
